,Liberal,,Samuel Walter Willet Pickup,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=a4d4148a-03d7-4f5a-a688-cca947fc6411&Language=E&Section=ALL
236149,ca.proc.d.1908-07-13.21.164,1908-07-13,05ffcd85-4168-4656-82c4-05a0c40faaae,ca.m.1687,Mr. EMMERSON.,,THE CANADA SHIPPING ACT.,,,If in 1896 we felt that the time had not-come when we should compel every man who navigated a vessel as far south as Cape Hatteras to have a certificate, the reasoning is so much the stronger.

,Liberal,,Henry Robert Emmerson,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=05ffcd85-4168-4656-82c4-05a0c40faaae&Language=E&Section=ALL
236150,ca.proc.d.1908-07-13.21.165,1908-07-13,a4d4148a-03d7-4f5a-a688-cca947fc6411,ca.m.4524,Mr. PICKUP.,,THE CANADA SHIPPING ACT.,,,You did not insist on their having certificates until 1903. Previous to 1903 certificates which were granted for coasting voyages enabled a master to sail a vessel to South America. It seems unfair to the man who gets a certificate now that he does not have the same privilege as the man who got a certificate previous to 1903.

,Liberal,,Samuel Walter Willet Pickup,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=a4d4148a-03d7-4f5a-a688-cca947fc6411&Language=E&Section=ALL
236151,ca.proc.d.1908-07-13.21.166,1908-07-13,05ffcd85-4168-4656-82c4-05a0c40faaae,ca.m.1687,Mr. EMMERSON.,,THE CANADA SHIPPING ACT.,,,For what reason did we limit it in 1903? I cannot conceive that this parliament would take such a step without some good and sufficient reason. I can only assume that the reason was that it was considered in the public interest that these vessels, when going on voyages south of Cape Hatteras, should be manned by officers who had certificates which were more than coastwise certificates.

,Liberal,,Henry Robert Emmerson,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=05ffcd85-4168-4656-82c4-05a0c40faaae&Language=E&Section=ALL
236152,ca.proc.d.1908-07-13.21.167,1908-07-13,d98b30ab-759a-4b5e-b3ba-420ce11b08d2,ca.m.9083,Mr. SINCLAIR.,,THE CANADA SHIPPING ACT.,,,I would like to know why my hon. friend wants to stop a coasting vessel at Cape Hatteras when its business is largely south of Cape Hatteras-in the West Indies. Why does he not want the vessel to go to some place where it can get some business, where our vessels have been going for generations? I venture to say that the hon. gentleman cannot find a single accident that has happened from the fact that coasting captains have been allowed to go south of Cape Hatteras. Everybody who has studied the question has felt that a mistake was made in 1903, when the limit was fixed at Cape Hatteras. I could understand a man saying that a vessel should not go around the Horn; but to say that we should stop at Cape Hatteras when a large amount of the business is done south of that point strikes me as absurd.

,Liberal,,John Howard Sinclair,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=d98b30ab-759a-4b5e-b3ba-420ce11b08d2&Language=E&Section=ALL
236153,ca.proc.d.1908-07-13.21.168,1908-07-13,05ffcd85-4168-4656-82c4-05a0c40faaae,ca.m.1687,Mr. EMMERSON.,,THE CANADA SHIPPING ACT.,,,We do not stop the business. We simply require that vessels engaging in that trade shall be manned by officers who have the necessary certificates.

,Liberal,,Henry Robert Emmerson,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=05ffcd85-4168-4656-82c4-05a0c40faaae&Language=E&Section=ALL
236154,ca.proc.d.1908-07-13.21.169,1908-07-13,d98b30ab-759a-4b5e-b3ba-420ce11b08d2,ca.m.9083,Mr. SINCLAIR.,,THE CANADA SHIPPING ACT.,,,You are defining the limits of a coasting voyage. Even whether a man has his certificate or not, he must stop when he reaches Cape Hatteras.

,Liberal,,John Howard Sinclair,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=d98b30ab-759a-4b5e-b3ba-420ce11b08d2&Language=E&Section=ALL
236155,ca.proc.d.1908-07-13.21.170,1908-07-13,05ffcd85-4168-4656-82c4-05a0c40faaae,ca.m.1687,Mr. EMMERSON.,,THE CANADA SHIPPING ACT.,,,But he can have a certificate otherwise than a coastwise certificate.

,Liberal,,Henry Robert Emmerson,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=05ffcd85-4168-4656-82c4-05a0c40faaae&Language=E&Section=ALL
236156,ca.proc.d.1908-07-13.21.171,1908-07-13,73436b70-d382-4eb3-9baf-bb0e92fdbf12,ca.m.1047,Mr. BRODEUR.,Minister of Marine and Fisheries,THE CANADA SHIPPING ACT.,,,My hon. friend knows that most of the mariners of the maritime provinces are coast-voyage mariners, and if you force them to take seaboard certificates, you will render matters more difficult for most of them.

,Liberal,,Louis-Philippe Brodeur,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=73436b70-d382-4eb3-9baf-bb0e92fdbf12&Language=E&Section=ALL
236157,ca.proc.d.1908-07-13.21.172,1908-07-13,0e4f9dca-5c4f-43d7-af07-16546fe9215d,ca.m.2882,Mr. J. D. REID.,,THE CANADA SHIPPING ACT.,,,I would ask the chairman for n ruling on the point I raised.

,Conservative (1867-1942),,John Dowsley Reid,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=0e4f9dca-5c4f-43d7-af07-16546fe9215d&Language=E&Section=ALL

,Liberal,,Samuel Walter Willet Pickup,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=a4d4148a-03d7-4f5a-a688-cca947fc6411&Language=E&Section=ALL

,Liberal,,Charles Marcil,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=8844037f-c912-404d-a505-6bf56321dd9a&Language=E&Section=ALL
236160,ca.proc.d.1908-07-13.21.175,1908-07-13,56fdc84e-aaff-46fe-bf93-d6f1014c6188,ca.m.519,Mr. A. K. MACLEAN.,,THE CANADA SHIPPING ACT.,,,Without speaking on the point of order, I would like to see the proposed legislation pass the House in one form or other, either as added sections to the government Bill or as it was introduced. It will take just as much time to-get it through later in the week as it will to-night. The minister could put himself in order bv changing a single word in the section which he asks to be added to the Bill. So I do not think my hon. friend should press his objection.

,Liberal,,Alexander Kenneth Maclean,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=56fdc84e-aaff-46fe-bf93-d6f1014c6188&Language=E&Section=ALL
236161,ca.proc.d.1908-07-13.21.176,1908-07-13,05ffcd85-4168-4656-82c4-05a0c40faaae,ca.m.1687,Mr. EMMERSON.,,THE CANADA SHIPPING ACT.,,,I wish it to be understood that I do not object to this amendment on the ground that it forms part of another Bill that stands on the Order Paper.

,Liberal,,Henry Robert Emmerson,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=05ffcd85-4168-4656-82c4-05a0c40faaae&Language=E&Section=ALL
236162,ca.proc.d.1908-07-13.21.177,1908-07-13,56fdc84e-aaff-46fe-bf93-d6f1014c6188,ca.m.519,Mr. A. K. MACLEAN.,,THE CANADA SHIPPING ACT.,,,I would ask my hon. friend to state his objection, so that we may know what it is, and then we can reply to it.

,Liberal,,Alexander Kenneth Maclean,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=56fdc84e-aaff-46fe-bf93-d6f1014c6188&Language=E&Section=ALL
236163,ca.proc.d.1908-07-13.21.178,1908-07-13,05ffcd85-4168-4656-82c4-05a0c40faaae,ca.m.1687,Mr. EMMERSON.,,THE CANADA SHIPPING ACT.,,,I do not object to the consideration of this clause, but I do object to changing the definition of the expression ' coasting trade ' so as to allow vessels manned by those having coastwise certificates going beyond the limitations set forth in the Act of 1903.

,Liberal,,Henry Robert Emmerson,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=05ffcd85-4168-4656-82c4-05a0c40faaae&Language=E&Section=ALL
236164,ca.proc.d.1908-07-13.21.179.1,1908-07-13,,,,stagedirection,,,,Amendment agreed to.,,,,
236165,ca.proc.d.1908-07-13.21.180,1908-07-13,73436b70-d382-4eb3-9baf-bb0e92fdbf12,ca.m.1047,Mr. BRODEUR.,Minister of Marine and Fisheries,THE CANADA SHIPPING ACT.,,,I would propose that section 3A be added to amend section 96 by striking out 100 and substituting 150. The Act provides that a sailing ship registered in Canada of 100 tons register may go to any port in Canada on a coasting voyage. I am now proposing to make the limit 150 tons.

,Liberal,,Louis-Philippe Brodeur,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=73436b70-d382-4eb3-9baf-bb0e92fdbf12&Language=E&Section=ALL

,Liberal,,Henry Robert Emmerson,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=05ffcd85-4168-4656-82c4-05a0c40faaae&Language=E&Section=ALL

Mr. BRODEUR moved that section 97 be amended by striking out the words * two hundred ' and substituting ' four hundred.'",,,,
236168,ca.proc.d.1908-07-13.21.183,1908-07-13,05ffcd85-4168-4656-82c4-05a0c40faaae,ca.m.1687,Mr. EMMERSON.,,THE CANADA SHIPPING ACT.,,,"I object to this increase.

,Liberal,,Henry Robert Emmerson,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=05ffcd85-4168-4656-82c4-05a0c40faaae&Language=E&Section=ALL
236169,ca.proc.d.1908-07-13.21.184,1908-07-13,73436b70-d382-4eb3-9baf-bb0e92fdbf12,ca.m.1047,Mr. BRODEUR.,Minister of Marine and Fisheries,THE CANADA SHIPPING ACT.,,,This is with regard to the mates.

,Liberal,,Louis-Philippe Brodeur,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=73436b70-d382-4eb3-9baf-bb0e92fdbf12&Language=E&Section=ALL
236170,ca.proc.d.1908-07-13.21.185,1908-07-13,05ffcd85-4168-4656-82c4-05a0c40faaae,ca.m.1687,Mr. EMMERSON.,,THE CANADA SHIPPING ACT.,,,The mate very often lias to take the place of the master. Frequently in voyages to the West Indies, the masters are lost at sea or die and the vessels have to be taken charge of by the mates. If there is any reason for requiring a certificated master, you should certainly require a certificated mate.

,Liberal,,Henry Robert Emmerson,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=05ffcd85-4168-4656-82c4-05a0c40faaae&Language=E&Section=ALL
236171,ca.proc.d.1908-07-13.21.186,1908-07-13,73436b70-d382-4eb3-9baf-bb0e92fdbf12,ca.m.1047,Mr. BRODEUR.,Minister of Marine and Fisheries,THE CANADA SHIPPING ACT.,,,As far as Great Britain is concerned, there is no restriction.

Every vessel engaged in such voyages may be without certificated officers. In the United States the restriction is 700 tons. Before the committee it was established by evidence that it was very difficult to find mates, and in some cases vessels had to be detained a long time because they could not get proper officers. We did not think it advisable to increase the limit to 700, but the committee thought we should Increase it to four hundred. With some reluctance, the department agreed to embody this clause In the Bill.

,Liberal,,Louis-Philippe Brodeur,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=73436b70-d382-4eb3-9baf-bb0e92fdbf12&Language=E&Section=ALL
236172,ca.proc.d.1908-07-13.21.187.1,1908-07-13,,,,stagedirection,,,,Amendment agreed to.,,,,
236173,ca.proc.d.1908-07-13.21.188,1908-07-13,dd99b0fc-3398-4c78-a44a-c8ff6a7e9f2e,ca.m.6832,Mr. KEMP.,,THE CANADA SHIPPING ACT.,,,Before the Bill leaves the committee, 1 would like to ask the minister a question. With respect to section 477 of the Bill-' compulsory payment of pilotage dues '-there are certain exemptions, as, for instance, certain vessels employed in voyages between ports on the great lakes and ports on the St. Lawrence. Were the representations made by the Dominion Marine Association considered, and what was done about them?

,Conservative (1867-1942),,Albert Edward Kemp,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=dd99b0fc-3398-4c78-a44a-c8ff6a7e9f2e&Language=E&Section=ALL
236174,ca.proc.d.1908-07-13.21.189,1908-07-13,73436b70-d382-4eb3-9baf-bb0e92fdbf12,ca.m.1047,*Mr. BRODEUR.,Minister of Marine and Fisheries,THE CANADA SHIPPING ACT.,,,Some representations were made by the Marine Association with regard to this. They asked that the Bill should be amended in tlie opposite direction from that we have taken. But I found on examining the records that it was impossible to comply with their request. I might quote several accidents that were due to the fact that the vessels had not proper pilots. There was one case that occurred this spring. My hon. friend understands the necessity there is of having vessels in charge of the right men on the St. Lawrence between Montreal and Quebec, the channel being somewhat narrow. Representations were made to me by the Shipping Federation that, in order to prevent accidents, we should always have pilots on these boats. The Shipping Federation represented to me the case of the ' John Lambert.' The master held a United States certificate and did not understand that toe rules for the harbour of . Montreal were different from those for the great lakes. The result of the captain not knowing this was a serious accident. Another instance was that of a young man who had been dismissed by the department as apprentice pilot because his habits were not regular, and who was taken to pilot some of these vessels. We have been taking all the precautions possible in order to ensure the safety of navigation of the St. Lawrence, and it would not do to allow a man who had been dismissed from the service because his habits were faulty to be taken on these boats and become the cause of accident.

236178,ca.proc.d.1908-07-13.21.193,1908-07-13,73436b70-d382-4eb3-9baf-bb0e92fdbf12,ca.m.1047,Mr. BRODEUR.,Minister of Marine and Fisheries,THE CANADA SHIPPING ACT.,,,This is a privilege not being taken advantage of by these people to whom it is allowed.

,Liberal,,Louis-Philippe Brodeur,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=73436b70-d382-4eb3-9baf-bb0e92fdbf12&Language=E&Section=ALL
236179,ca.proc.d.1908-07-13.21.194,1908-07-13,dd99b0fc-3398-4c78-a44a-c8ff6a7e9f2e,ca.m.6832,Mr. KEMP.,,THE CANADA SHIPPING ACT.,,,But it is a very serious matter for the captains of vessels on the great lakes who are trying to build up trade between the upper lakes and the lower ports. I will not take up time discussing the matter ; I simply enter my protest against it.
Bill reported.

,Liberal,,Sydney Arthur Fisher,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=8898cbb9-c7b4-4b1d-8019-f6672fcd0560&Language=E&Section=ALL

236193,ca.proc.d.1908-07-13.22.13,1908-07-13,9b9087eb-6add-462b-bc28-48898b45eb69,ca.m.4640,Mr. ARMSTRONG.,,SUPPLY.,,,I have been waiting for an opportunity to comment on the humiliating manner in which the Minister of Agriculture has treated the Agricultural Committee and the members of this House. It is not reasonable to make any prolonged discussion in regard to agricultural matters at this stage of the session. But I want to call the attention of the minister to the way he has treated the Agricultural Committee, and the way in which he has dealt with the resolution that committee passed on the 20th June, 1905. That resolution read as follows :

That this committee realize an injustice is being done to the people of Canada through their British embargo on our cattle being maintained, and believe that it would be in the best interests of the farming industry of the Dominion to have a deputation consisting of the Minister of Agriculture of each province of the Dominion to act in conjunction with the Dominion Minister of Agriculture to wait upon the chairman of the Board of Agriculture of England, giving as much publicity to their proceedings as possible, and laying before the said department the justice of our requests, to have the Act authorising the said embargo repealed.

That resolution went through committee into this House, and the House passed it unanimously. It was the wish of both sides of the House that the minister should coil-duct that matter in the manner expressed in the resolution. Now he has not raised a finger towards carrying out the wishes of this House. In his reply to this resolution he makes use of the following words :

The Minister of Agriculture has made no effort to bring together such a deputation for the purpose set forth in the above resolution, for the reason that, in view of the repeated representations made by the Canadian government and the persistent refusals of the British government (as shown by the documents attached hereto and those previously Mr. FOWLER.

brought down) and the persistent action of the British parliament in refusing to amend the existing law so as to admit of the importation of live Canadian oattle into the United Kingdom, such action would, in his opinion, be futile and undignified.

Why does the minister take the position that it would be both futile and undignified to obey a resolution of this House ? He takes the position that the Agricultural Committee and the members of this House did not know what they were doing when they passed that resolution. I could go through the whole of this correspondence relating to the cattle embargo, and show that the minister has not raised a finger towards trying to remove that cattle embargo. I have letters under my hand addressed to Lord Strathcona wherein he states distinctly that so far as this government is concerned they do not want to get mixed up with the cattle embargo in Great Britain. When he received letters from the meat association of Great Britain, and when he knew that an agitation was going on in that country from year to year, and he was urged to give some encouragement to those who were endeavouring to remove the cattle embargo, the minister, instead of giving that encouragement, did the very opposite, and would not give a particle of encouragement to these men. The minister knows that when the vote was taken in the British House of Commons his attention was called to it ; he knows that when representations were made to him from different sections of the country urging him to lend some assistance to the men who were fighting for the removal of the cattle embargo in Great Britain, he refused to raise a finger, he practically told Lord Strathcona that this government did not wish any action to be taken.

Mr. Fisher wrote as follows:

My Dear Lord Strathcona,-Yours of October 11 has just come before me. I have been away for several weeks in the west arid only private letters were forwarded to me. I note what you say in regard to the cattle embargo discussion. It seems to me in line with our opinion that we ought not to take any part in this, which has now reached the stage of a political discussion in England. I would not suggest your having anything to do with the conference. Of course, if matters there develop so as to make you decide it worth your while to do anything about it, I shall be quite satisfied to leave that to your judgment.

And so on. il have here a memorial from the National Federation of the Meat Trader's Association which I might read for the benefit of the Canadian people who take an interest in this question, but the time is too limited. I would like however to just call attention of the minister to another letter which he wrote Lord Strathcona on the 10th May, 1905. I shall only read a part of it because it is very lengthy.

I do not know Mr. M. Donald Munro, but it is well understood that the men who handle Canadian fat cattle, shipping them to England are not particular about the embargo being removed. The farmers of this country, however, are, and there is a general feeling in the country on the 'part of everybody that the embargo is unjust and reflects upon the health of our cattle. . . .

I feel that we Canadians ought not to enter at all into the controversy at present going on in England, and therefore I have made no reference to any of the articles which appeared in the press there or the statements which were made by public men, with the single exception of what appeared to be in the official utterances of the minister.

I might go on reading letter after letter to show that the minister, instead of coming out boldly on the question and taking an active interest in it, instead of putting forth his best efforts to have the cattle embargo removed, was devoting his attention to minor matters. I only wish I had time to go

on and show the futile part the minister has taken in this whole matter. If I had the time I could go on and show what little interest he has taken in a subject which is so vital to agricultural interests. Take his whole career during the past eleven years and you will find that instead of his paying attention to the development of that great cattle industry, he has been paying his attention to some of the other departments to the neglect of the greatest industry we have. When we look over the paltry bits of legislation he has brought in for the advantage as he deems it, of our agricultural industry, we cannot but be convinced that the time cannot come too soon when a different government will have control of the country and promote different legislation for the advancement of that great interest.

Every year we pn this side have tried to impress the minister with the necessity of increasing the quantity of grain sent as a sample. We carry on farming differently in Manitoba from the way it is carried on in the eastern provinces. When only a small quantity of seed 'is sent to a farmer it is almost impossible for him to keep it separate.

If a farmer has a bushel, or sufficient to sow an acre, then he is in a position to harvest that and keep it by itself, and when he comes to thresh it, It will not be mixed up with other kinds of grain. It would be better if the minister would send out this seed to fewer persons and send it in larger quantities. A farmer in a particular district would get sufficient to seed an acre or two, and then after a year he is in a position to supply his neighbours with that kind of seed. I am glad to hear that the minister is going to be more liberal in sending out the synopsis that he has published. Some time ago I called his attention to the necessity of placing these books in the hands of the various municipal councils throughout the country. Since then I have had a great many letters from the clerks of municipal councils in the province of Manitoba, and from reeves, asking that this book might be placed in the municipal offices, the same as the minister has been distributing them among the various school districts. I would ask him now if it is his intention to carry out that idea?

We have an item of $18,000 for the production and use of superior seeds, and for the enforcement of the Seeds Control Act. We might cut that item in two, and I would like to know what could be accomplished by $9,000 in encouraging the production and use of superior seeds of farm crops. The government should send out fewer seeds in sufficient quantity to enable the farmers to bring forth good seed. We know that even when good seed is sown on a farm for a number of years it deteriorates. If the government were to spend $100,000 in sending out larger quantities of seed, they would be doing the greatest possible benefit to the farmers. In my experience I have had great trouble in supplying the farmers who wrote to me asking for samples of seed. I received a number of letters asking for this seed, and I got two or three samples and could not get any more. The farmers are the most important class in this country, and this item should not be less than $100,000.

For a number of years in different parts of Canada there were local stud books and herd books kept for registering the pedigree of animals, but this system was found to be detrimental to the breeders of live stock, because a pedigree issued in Quebec would not be recognized in Ontario or the other provinces, and a pedigree issued in Ontario

would, In the same way, not be recognized outside of that province. Representatives of the breeders and live stock throughout the Dominion held a convention in Ottawa and they asked the Department of Agriculture to establish national stud books and herd books. After a great deal of discussion and consideration, I agreed to allow the National Live Stock Association to establish records and books at Ottawa, and I gave them office room in the department. It was agreed that the department should affix the Dominion stamp to the certificates they issued declaring that these records were accepted by the Department of Agriculture. At first all the breeders did not fall in with the arrangement, but one after another they have asked to be included in these national records, and among others the French Canadian Horse Breeders' Association. I discussed the matter with the breeders of French Canadian horses and we found that a great many animals had been recorded which were not French Canadian at all, and had no affinity with the French Canadian breed. In the province of Quebec the French Canadian breed of horses used to be well known, but unfortunately it has almost disappeared and there are very few pure bred animals left. In their anxiety to get a pedigree for their horses a number of French Canadian farmers had them registered in the Quebec book. Some of them were no more French Canadian horses than would be an English thoroughbred. Some of them were actually registered in other stud books as being standard bred trotters, some of them even as Clydesdales or English thoroughbreds. 236322,ca.proc.d.1908-07-13.22.142,1908-07-13,5970b6f2-6f2a-4c89-bd5d-8a640dc3a4aa,ca.m.9247,Mr. W. JACKSON.,,SUPPLY.,,,There has been some discussion to-night in reference to the embargo. That is a question we cannot settle in the way we would, as we have to deal with a country outside of our own. I am not in favour, and I do not think the average farmer in Canada is in favour, of having our beef manufactured in England. We should finish the beef in Canada, and it seems to me that if we had regulations so that when our finished cattle went to England they could be retained there for a time before being slaughtered, it would be a great advantage; because cattle after crossing the ocean, and perhaps having a bad voyage, are not in fit shape to be slaughtered on arrival. Our live-stock goes to Great Britain under the same regulations as live-stock from the United States. Three or four years ago the British government prohibited cattle from going from a certain part of the United States. It was during the winter, when our cattle were practically barred from going to England, because they were shipped via the short line, which passes through the State of Maine, and we were prohibited from using that road, which practically meant that we had not that outlet for our stock. But bad as this embargo is, the agriculturist of this country must be vigilant to retain the privilege we have in the old country to-day. Our cattle are going through the United States to the British market and American cattle are going through Canada to the British market; and if there is any ground, however frail it may be, for the British agriculturist to say, the cattle from Canada and the United States are diseased, we shall find our cattle placed on the same footing as the Argentine cattle. Therefore we must be watchful of the privilege we have in getting our cattle into Great Britain in the way we do. But there is one thing which we have under our own control, and that is the right and privilege of improving our beef producing cattle, it is a regrettable thing to find in the weekly reports of the British market that our Canadian Mr. FISHER.

cattle are quoted at from a half cent to a cent a pound lower than American cattle. The result is that the British agriculturist who desires to seek a home outside of England will conclude that there is something wrong with the agricultural area of Canada, and will prefer to go to the United States; whereas as a matter of fact the conditions in Canada are such that we can produce better beef than they do in the United States. We can go to the United States fat stock shows and take all the first prizes.

The trouble with our cattle is they are not uniform. Our agriculturists look with pride to the stand our cheese has taken in the old country. Is it not in their interest that our cheese should be rated there as high a3 it is? If that be the case with cheese, it is more so in the ease of cattle. It is highly desirable that our cattle should enjoy the same high standard. While our Agricultural Department has not possibly given too much attention to the cheese producing breeds of cattle, they have not given the attention they should have to the beef producers. We are losing millions of dollars every year through not producing higher grades of beef cattle. I have watched some of the experiments on the farm, perhaps more particularly since I have been in this House, and I must say that the last report of that department has been more to my taste and fancy than any of the previous ones. Our farmers are not as well convinced as they should be that they are losing money by feeding second-class grades instead of first-class stock, and I would like to ask the minister what he is doing in his department to improve the beef producing of cattle in Canada.

236323,ca.proc.d.1908-07-13.22.143,1908-07-13,8898cbb9-c7b4-4b1d-8019-f6672fcd0560,ca.m.110,Mr. FISHER.,Minister of Agriculture,SUPPLY.,,,One of the first things we undertook to do was to work in connection with the administration of the different fairs throughout the country and endeavoured to get a definite line of prizes and a definite and uniform system of judging. For that purpose we have sent out judges-not all of the officers of the department-to different fairs and we pay the travelling expenses of these men. The result has been a great improvement in the quality of judging. We have gone further in making these judges give their reasons verbally in the ring for their decisions so that the competitors will understand why one animal is so much better than another. That has a very good educative effect, and we have been very much gratified to find that an increasing number of exhibitions all over the country are asking for these expert judges. The extent to which they have done that, shows the value of the work. We have also had a system by which we have aided in the sales of thoroughbred bulls. Where the associations undertake to have a sale of thoroughbred bulls, we sometimes send an expert to aid in selecting the bulls and in other cases give small amounts to these

associations to assist them in carrying on the sales, by means of which a superior class of male animals has been distributed. Not always the highest clfiss because we cannot as a rule have these sold at auction as the breeders of the choicest animals prefer to sell by private sale; but still we have been able by these means to assist in the introduction of a better breed of animals to be utilized for the improvement of the common cattle and in that way raise the quality of the stock. For instance in this particular neighbourhood of Ottawa, some five or six years ago it was almost impossible for a farm manager to buy fifty or sixty steers in the fall for the purpose of fattening, but to-day he has no difficulty getting them in this neighbourhood, thus showing an improvement in the live stock, and that is true of almost every part of Canada.

I regret very much at this early hour of the morning, and this late stage of the session, that I should feel obliged to discuss any matter of importance, but as the question I wish to discuss relates to the imprisonment of a man who, in the opinion of a great many of his friends, has been unjustly deprived of his liberty, I think it is of sufficient importance to devote a few moments to the consideration of it. Frederick Blunden, who lived in the neighbourhood of Fort Macleod, was tried there on November 22nd, 1904, and convicted of stealing two steers, and has been imprisoned at Macleod and Edmonton for three years and a half. Ever since his incarceration he has been appealing to the Department of Justice for a new trial. He objected to appeal for executive clemency, because he insisted that he was entirely innocent of the charge upon which he was convicted, and it would not answer his ends to fe pardoned or allowed out on ticket-of-leave. These appeals have come, as the papers have shown, at intervals ever since his incarceration. The oue answer has been sent to him-that nothing could be done. Now, it would be necessary to enter shortly into the evidence given at that trial in order to show why I differ, in some sense, from the Minister of Justice (Mr. Aylesworth) and ' his predecessor. I do so with a great deal

of diffidence, because, with my limited experience, it hardly becomes me to differ with gentlemen who have had so much experience in these matters. The trial took place before Mr. Justice Harvey at Fort Macleod. The only evidence that was given against Blunden was that of Richard Train, who was caught by the Northwest Mounted Police killing these two cattle. Train's explanation of the matter at the time the mounted police came down upon him was that he had purchased the cattle two months before from a man he did not know. He repeated that on two occasions to -the two sergeants of police, and he also said that if he had made a mistake he was quite willing to pay for the steers. Train was put in jail at Fort Macleod and lay there twenty-eight days before he made any charge against Blunden. Then, according to the evidence which is under my hand, he stated -that he made this charge to save himself and by the advice of his ' agent '- I suppose he means his solicitor. This evidence of Train was contradicted in one very important particular by one of his own hired men. I might go back for a moment to explain that the story told by Train at the trial was that on Sunday evening, four days before he killed the cattle, Blunden took tea with him in the presence of his two hired men. During the course of the meal Blunden said he had one steer to sell. After eating tea, Train says, they went out together behind the barn, and Blunden pointed out in the bunch of cattle, from 100 to 200-Train said he would not swear there were not 200-these two steers. Train admits that he was not within fifty yards of the cattle, and says that Blunden rode down on his horse and pointed out two cattle in the bunch as cattle which he was willing to sell. Train admitted that it was dusk and almost dark. It seemed absurd to think that a man could distinguish a couple of cattle in a bunch of 200 when he was fifty yards away. The contradictioin to this statement is in the evidence of Lewis Albert Carr. His evidence showed clearly that he was trying to screen Train. His evidence, as given at page 75, showed that he was at Train's on the 11th September, the day this is said to have taken place. Then, at page 70 :

Q. You mean Blunden went out before you did or after?-A. Before I did.

I did not mention that Train was convicted before Judge Scott of stealing two other cattle and sentenced to five years imprisonment, whereas Judge Harvey sen-sentenced this man against whom, as I con' tend, there was no proof, to double that term. Although I have failed so far with my hon. friend the Minister of Justice to get any reconsideration of the case, I trust that he will be able to take a different view of the matter and to grant the prayer of the petition and of the man who has written to him so often upon this subject.

In regard to the conduct of Blunden in prison, I might mention that the reports of his conduct have been from the first satisfactory and that in the last two reports he is recommended strongly as a proper subject for the consideration of the department. I would ask the minister to consider whether this is not a proper case for intervention. This man, although he has been invited, as the correspondence will show, to apply for executive clemency, states that he wants a new trial in order to establish his innocence and to go out a free man instead of a man with a stigma upon him. Surely it is some evidence of the innocence of this man that he refuses to apply for executive clemency, states that he wants a new trial in order to establish his innocence and to go out a free man instead of a man with a stigma upon him. Surely it is some evidence of the innocence of this man that he refuses to apply for executive clemency. It is some evidence of his innocence that he Mr. WARD.

desires, in view of the new evidence which has come to light, that he shall be given an opportunity of showing that he was not guilty in the first place. In that connection I have an affidavit here from a man named Samuel Nelson, of Granum, dated February 13 last, which states that on or before September 14, he met Richard N, Train, with his boy driving a bunch of cattle between Round lake and Rocky coulee. My hon. friend from Alberta (Mr. Herron) can give you information as to where that is. They were going in the direction of Train's home, Rocky coulee. This was on the day before Train was discovered killing these cattle and the evidence shows clearly, in fact, Train says, that these cattle were driven in by his boy and his girl. It is stated in one of the letters to the minister that this boy and girl of Train's would swear, if they had an opportunity, that these cattle that they drove in were cattle that Blunden never had anything to do with. In the face of all the evidence that has been presented, I would simply ask the minister to reconsider his decision not to grant a new trial and if that cannot be done, why, I suppose the only thing for Blunden to do is to apply for executive clemency. The man, is far gone in consumption and it will be a blot upon the administration of the department if he should die during his term of imprisonment.

236336,ca.proc.d.1908-07-13.22.156,1908-07-13,4080fe01-bb47-413a-8f32-e4f7c4c4c3de,ca.m.6099,Mr. HERRON.,,SUPPLY.,,,I wish to say a word in reference to the matter. As the case has been so fully dealt with by my hon. friend from Durham (Mr. Ward) I shall not at this late hour attempt to cover the ground again. The hon. gentleman has dealt with certain circumstances which led up to the conviction of Blunden so fully that the committee will thoroughly understand the situation. I would like to say a word further in connection with what led up to the severity of the judge in this case. I am not going to complain of the action of the judge in any way. For about ten or twenty years cattle stealing had been going on practically all the time all over the country and it seemed impossible to convict any one of this offence. It assumed such proportions that the whole country was up in arms against it, all the [DOT] respectable people of that country, the officers of the law and even the judges, but they did not like to undertake to prosecute men on the ordinary evidence as compared with evidence that might be used in similar cases in other parts of the country. For the last ten years this cattle stealing has been going on to such an extent that the judges have almost reversed the transaction and now they are in many eases over severe. They are ready to convict men who have been accused of cattle and horse stealing on very slight evidence, and sometimes for the sake of getting a conviction they will accept evidence that they would not ac-

cept under ordinary circumstances. That is what has led up to this. I have no doubt that while judges have leaned towards leniency they have on occasions gone to extremes the other way. There is no fault of course to be found with the judge in this case. I hope the Minister of Justice will give this matter his serious consideration and if he gives this man a new trial he will be acting in accordance with the opinion of 95 per cent of the respectable people in that country. A great many people believe that Blunden is an innocent man. From the evidence it will be seen that it is quite possible that the man Train endeavoured to save himself by giving false evidence against Blunden. I believe Blunden is an innocent man and I hope the minister will give him a new trial and an opportunity to establish his innocence.

,Liberal-Conservative,,John Herron,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=4080fe01-bb47-413a-8f32-e4f7c4c4c3de&Language=E&Section=ALL
236337,ca.proc.d.1908-07-13.22.157,1908-07-13,f086f57f-8342-4b2e-819a-37713991d665,ca.m.6610,Mr. AYLESWORTH.,Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada,SUPPLY.,,,When the hon. member for Durham (Mr. Ward) moved some months ago for the papers in this matter I urged that in the interests of the prisoner himself the motion should not be pressed. I am still very strongly of opinion that cases of prisoners who are universally making application for clemency or reconsideration of their trials should not be made the subject of discussion in parliament. The file in this case consists of some 300 or 400 pages and my hon. friend (Mr. Ward) has examined it and is familiar with it. I have read it some time ago and I am somewhat familiar with the circumstances, but other members of the committee are necessarily not acquainted with the facts. I do not propose to discuss them because they certainly cannot be intelligently discussed within a few minutes. Each of these two men had his trial, before a different judge, and each judge came to a like conclusion with regard to the guilt of each man. Neither was tried with a jury but two different judges upon different occasions and upon facts that to some extent differed, was distinctly of opinion that each man was guilty of the offence charged. My hon. friend has seen the confidential report of the judge before whom Blunden was tried and the judge says that he was convinced the man was guilty upon his own cross-examination. I can only say that after considering and reading the testimony so far from being convinced of the prisoner's innocence I have arrived at an opposite conclusion. Of course it is impossible for one who simply reads the evidence, to come to any conclusion at all as satisfactory upon a pure question of fact as the judge can who sees and hears the witnesses. I can see no reason why the conclusion of an experienced judge upon such a question of fact ought not to be deemed as valuable as the conclusion of a jury, or ought to be interferred with any more lightly. With one breath it is said that this prisoner insists upon his innocence and does not ask clemency while with another it is urged that it is a case in which clemency ought to be exercised. The prisoner himself is not by any means as unbending as my hon. friend from Durham puts it, because he has distinctly asked for clemency.

,Liberal,,Allen Bristol Aylesworth,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=f086f57f-8342-4b2e-819a-37713991d665&Language=E&Section=ALL

,Conservative (1867-1942),,Henry Alfred Ward,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=6fdf3fe2-5341-459d-bcf2-ff92e4977bdc&Language=E&Section=ALL
236339,ca.proc.d.1908-07-13.22.159,1908-07-13,f086f57f-8342-4b2e-819a-37713991d665,ca.m.6610,Mr. AYLESWORTH.,Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada,SUPPLY.,,,It is true he maintains his innocence, but he urges his release upon the ground that he has served a long imprisonment already and ought to be the subject of a pardon or of conditional release upon ticket of leave. That is something in regard to which discretion has to be exercised, and I express no other opinion than to say that in view of the circumstances of the case it has seemed to me up to this time at any rate that it would be premature to interfere, and I have been unable to see my way to recommend it. On the question of a new trial I want to say merely a word. I do not understand the law to be that there is resting upon the Minister of Justice any duty or any right to order a new trial because the man convicted asks for it. I think the statute does not mean anything of the sort. We are here with the British system of administering criminal justice under which we have absolutely no provision whatever for the giving of a new trial by the courts in criminal eases, on a question of fact. If there is a mistake in law it is a different thing; if there is a mistake on the part of the learned judge in laying down the law to the jury or if there is legal miscarriage there is provision for a new trial. Can it be that the same parliament which so deliberately declined to intrust to any court in the country the power to order a new trial in criminal cases on a question of fact, would vest that very power in the uncontrolled discretion of a Minister of Justice.
I think it would be extraordinary if that were the law. Now, if we look at the section in the Criminal Code which is relied on, I think it plainly does not mean anything of the sort. It says :
column2: If (not upon

column1: the application of the prisoner) but if, upon an application for the clemency of the Crown in favour of some person convicted of a crime the Minister of Justice feels doubt whether this person ought to have been found guilty, he may, instead of recommending His Majesty to pardon or commute the sentence, after such inquiry as he thinks fit, order in writing that a new trial be had, at such time and before such court as he thinks right. It is not upon an application which the prisoner makes as a matter of right or as a matter of indulgence that a new trial may be given to him, but it is upon an application for clemency. It never could have been intended that any man, by the device of asking for clemency, could in an indirect way ask for a new trial. It is something of the minister's own

motion which is contemplated by the statute. If the minister, in considering an application for clemency, feels so much doubt about the matter that he does not know what to do. then of his own accord he may take this course as a solution of the difficulty. What would you have if it were otherwise ? This is a provision not limited to capital cases or to important cases of any kind, or to cases involving long imprisonment, but extending to every criminal prosecution, every petty squabble before a magistrate ; and if the Minister of Justice has power to grant a new trial in all criminal cases upon being asked to do so, it means that one man is appointed in Ottawa to sit in review over the hundreds and thousands of criminal cases which are tried every day of the week and in all parts of this country from the Atlantic to the Pacific. I think the simple stating of the thing demonstrates that it never was intended by parliament. No court may do it in any province, but one man is to sit in Ottawa and do that work for the whole Dominion. It is an impossible thing on the face of it, because when you once started doing it, you would have an application after every conviction. But apart from that there is no machinery for it. Suppose the prosecutor refused to attend ; there is no means of bringing him before this august tribunal *which is to sit on his cause. And how is the minister to proceed ? No Indication is given in the statute. I can only say that having given, not this particular case, but various capital cases, the most anxious consideration, my mind is unalterably convinced that parliament never intended to vest such jurisdiction in the Minister of Justice. In capital cases it has come to be almost universal that the prisoner's counsel applies for a new trial under this section, insisting that there has been something wrong done by the jury, that there was some evidence which was not correct, that there is something 'new discovered; and the counsel thinks it is a dreadful thing for the Minister of Justice to tell him, what I am saying to-night, that he does not believe that parliament ever intended to vest any such, power in the Minister of Justice. I think it would be disastrous to the administration of criminal justice in this country if it were so. I may say that ever since this section has been on the statute-book, in only one instance has it been acted upon, and that was one in which there was a lamentable miscarriage of justice. How could it be otherwise ? Suppose that a prisoner was convicted and condemned after a long trial by a jury, and then on an application the Minister of Justice sets aside the verdict and orders a new trial. Every juryman at the new trial would know it. There would be the argument almost irresistible that this great potentate had felt that the verdict against the prisoner was so unjust that he would not allow it to stand, and or-Mr. AYLESWORTH.

dered a new trial. It is tantamount to an instruction to the new jury to acquit. In the case mentioned it was so taken ; there was an acquittal in spite of clear evidence. With regard to the case of this prisoner, I can only say that it is plain that although the other man may afterwards have been convicted of a like offence, it does not establish the innocence of the man against whom he testified. On the contrary, as the judge in Train's case pointed out, it might well be on all the testimony that both men were guilty, and indeed that was his opinion. The Minister of Justice must treat these cases when they come before him as applications for clemency, as cases in which the prisoner was properly convicted. He looks about for extenuating circumstances, inquires into all the facts of the case, the man's previous character, and taking into account all these considerations he advises whether or not it is a case in which the sentence, though it is a proper one, can properly be interfered with ; and it is upon that view and upon that only that his recommendations to His Excellency must proceed.
